multi-seed/checkpoint averaging, score/rank voting, mixtures of independently fitted
experts, or neural scores combined with separately fitted transition/popularity scores.

Jointly trained internal layers/features of one network are allowed. Four category
models are necessary for routing and do not constitute an ensemble. All hypotheses,
code generation, debugging, reviews and memory use must respect this constraint even
if an upstream generic prompt suggests an ensemble. The host audits the actual
predictor before accepting validation scores; violations fail the trial and consume

 ## Search results
[Correcting the LogQ Correction (RecSys 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331) is the closest match for sampled-softmax bias: the positive target is included deterministically, whereas negatives are sampled. Its refined derivation separates these contributions and introduces an uncertainty-dependent sample weight; reported improvements concern retrieval/sequential models, not this BERT4Rec benchmark. [Scalable Cross-Entropy (RecSys 2024)](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/5392aca9-0bae-4176-9b3a-a8165957ba26) offers another direction: approximate catalog softmax using GPU-efficient selection of high-scoring outputs, concentrating computation on informative competitors.

For false-negative control, [Adaptive Hardness Negative Sampling (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28709) argues that fixed hardness creates false-positive/false-negative problems and adapts hardness during training; evidence is collaborative filtering rather than BERT4Rec. [EMM (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608026004090) combines refreshed candidate memory, hard-negative mining, a small random mix, and safeguards excluding positive IDs and overly similar candidates. Its experiments use graph recommenders, so transfer to masked sequential prediction remains unverified.

Practical hypothesis: preserve one bidirectional BERT4Rec per category and compare corrected stochastic sampled softmax against a conservative random/semi-hard mixture, excluding targets and observed training positives. Warm up before increasing hardness; avoid concentrating exclusively on the highest-scoring negatives. These are proposed adaptations, not demonstrated gains for Industrial_and_Scientific or Electronics. Deterministic top-k mining changes the proposal distribution, so ordinary logQ correction cannot automatically be treated as valid. Select using the fixed four-category macro validation HR@10 while retaining masked-target training and appended-mask inference.

---

BERT4Rec’s objective mismatch is established, and terminal masking is already part of the original method: §3.6 explicitly adds training examples masking only the last item to better match appended-mask inference. Thus, increasing terminal-mask exposure is a grounded hypothesis, rather than a new architectural departure. Recency Sampling also argues that random item masking is weakly aligned with sequential recommendation, although its reported improvements concern other backbones. [Original BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690v2), [Recency Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643).

Practical experiment, inferred from these findings: jointly train one bidirectional BERT4Rec with random-mask reconstruction and terminal-mask prediction on sampled training-history prefixes. For terminal examples, choose target x_t, provide only [x_1,…,x_{t−1},MASK], and optimize cross-entropy at MASK; exclude x_t and all later events from that input. Mix these examples with ordinary masked reconstruction, or increase their share late in training. Normalize the two losses separately so numerous reconstruction targets do not overwhelm terminal supervision. Preserve left padding and read the final nonpadding MASK position. These sources do not establish an optimal mixing weight or guarantee improvement on the four Amazon categories.

Related recent evidence: Masked History Learning (September 2025; revised April 2026) combines historical reconstruction with next-item prediction and a curriculum shifting toward future prediction. It supports testing complementary objectives, but studies generative recommendation, so its gains do not directly validate this BERT4Rec adaptation. [MHL paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23649).

---

Temporal modeling offers the clearest transferable ideas. [TemProxRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09784) incorporates temporal proximity through self-attention and contrastive learning; [TLSTSRec (online 2024)](https://doi.org/10.3233/IDA-240051) combines long- and short-term temporal information with adaptive fusion. A directly relevant [BERT4Rec session-enhancement paper (2026)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01554-z) describes a bidirectional masked backbone, a short-session representation weighted by continuous time decay and content relevance, and learned gating between recent and historical interests. These suggest jointly trained temporal attention and recent-history pooling within one BERT4Rec network. The older [TiSASRec paper](https://jiachengli1995.github.io/files/wsdm20.pdf) provides explicit interval-aware attention equations; its temporal mechanism could be adapted without adopting its causal backbone.

Evidence for lightweight text encoders trained entirely from scratch was weaker in the retrieved results. [CALRec (RecSys 2024)](https://research.google/pubs/calrec-contrastive-alignment-of-generative-llms-for-sequential-recommendation/) jointly aligns user histories and item descriptions, but depends on pretrained PaLM-2 and therefore does not satisfy this task’s constraints. A plausible experiment—not an established result from these papers—is a small randomly initialized token embedding table with mean pooling or a shallow CNN over titles/descriptions, projected into the item-ID space and optimized jointly with masked-item prediction. Share this item representation between history encoding and candidate scoring, and learn temporal attention within the same checkpoint.
